Chapter 3: Permission to Create Comes from Within, Not from Others
Let’s talk about something that quietly holds a lot of us back—this idea that we need permission from someone else to be creative. Sound familiar? Maybe you’ve caught yourself waiting for a sign, or hoping someone will tell you, “Go ahead, you’ve got what it takes.”
Most of us pick up this habit early, whether it’s from our childhood or just the world around us. But here’s the truth: no one else can give you the right to create. That’s something you have to claim for yourself.
Imagine someone who’s always wanted to paint. Years go by, and they keep telling themselves it’s not the right time, or they don’t have enough talent, or nobody’s cheering them on. But that itch to create never really goes away. Then, after a tough week, they find themselves in an art supply store—almost by accident—and walk out with a set of paints. No plan, no audience, and no idea if it’ll lead anywhere. Just a quiet, private choice to finally give it a try.
Of course, those first paintings don’t look the way they hoped. Things feel awkward and maybe even a bit embarrassing. The temptation to quit is strong. But something surprising happens: just the act of making, of putting brush to canvas, brings a kind of satisfaction they didn’t expect. Suddenly, it’s clear—the only permission that matters is the one you give yourself. The willingness to try, to mess up, and to keep going.
So many people fall into the trap of waiting for approval. Whether it’s from teachers, friends, or even strangers, we hope someone will let us know our work is good enough. But here’s something to pay attention to—external praise can be uplifting one day, and gone the next. If you hang your hopes on it, you’ll always be chasing something you can’t control.
Living creatively takes a different kind of courage. It’s about trusting yourself—over and over again—because what you’re making matters to you. It’s not about thinking you’re better than anyone else. It’s about quietly saying, “I’m allowed to try, even if nobody else gets it.”
There’s another story I love. Picture a parent who, after years of putting everyone else first, decides to start taking photos. Friends and family don’t really see the point. “Why bother?” they ask. But this parent keeps going, snapping pictures of little daily moments. Over time, those photos become a cherished record—a way of really seeing and appreciating life. It wasn’t about getting likes or applause; it was just about giving themselves permission to notice and create.
Most of us don’t realize that waiting for permission is actually a way to protect ourselves. It feels safer to blame a lack of opportunity than to risk failing or being disappointed. But think about what’s lost—how many unfinished ideas, or dreams, never get a chance just because we’re waiting for someone else to say “yes.”
Here’s the key takeaway: creative living is all about self-authorization. It’s the decision to participate, to make, and to share—no matter what comes of it. And this isn’t a one-time thing. You’ll need to grant yourself that permission again and again, in small everyday ways. Eventually, it becomes a habit—a way of moving through life with more openness and curiosity.
